property_summary: After calling go() with any nonzero value, the contract's balance is forwarded entirely to owner so address(c).balance == 0.

For all calls to go(amount), the original contract always reverts if the target address would reject calls with empty calldata, so the mutant (which sends non-empty calldata) can change whether go reverts; the test asserts that go must always revert for the provided amount.
When go() is called with any wei, the contract C always ends with zero balance (it forwards any received Ether to owner even if the external call fails).
Calling go(...) always reverts when the external call to target fails (so if the target call would fail, go must revert).
If calling go(...) does not revert then C's balance must be zero afterwards (i.e., successful go never leaves Ether in the contract).
If go(...) call does not revert, then address(c).balance equals 0 and the call did not consume the sent ether (i.e., the caller's balance decreased by the sent amount).

property_summary: If c.go(amount) does not revert then address(c).balance must be 0 after the call (i.e., successful go forwards any held ether out).

For any caller and any ETH value sent to go(), the reference contract always forwards any remaining contract balance to owner (so address(c).balance == 0 after go()); the mutant that ignores a failing external call can leave funds in the contract when that external call reverts, violating this rule for some inputs.

For any caller and any ETH amount sent to go(), the correct contract always ends with zero balance (it forwards remaining balance to owner); the mutant that ignores a failing external call can leave ETH stuck in the contract when the external call to the adversarial callee reverts, so there exist inputs (an amount and using a reverting callee address) that make the mutant retain nonzero balance.

For every call to go() with any msg.value and any callee address, the reference C always ends with zero contract balance (it forwards remaining balance to owner); the mutant that ignores a failing external call can leave ETH stuck in the contract when the external call to a callee reverts, so there exist inputs (a msg.value and a reverting callee deployed and used as the target) that make the mutant retain nonzero balance.

For every call to go() with any msg.value and any callee address deployed as the target, the reference contract always ends with zero balance (it forwards remaining balance to owner); the mutant that ignores a failing external call can leave ETH stuck in the contract when the callee reverts, so there exist inputs (a positive msg.value and a deployed reverting callee used as the target) that make the mutant retain a nonzero balance, violating the rule.

For every nonzero msg.value sent to go() when the callee address is a deployed contract that reverts on receiving ETH, the reference C will forward any remaining balance out (leaving address(c).balance == 0) because it reverts on failed call, whereas the mutant that ignores the failed call can end with a nonzero contract balance for some fuzzed amounts and a reverting callee.

For any call to go() forwarding some ETH to the external target that succeeds, the contract's owner address retains the ETH forwarded back from C (address(c).balance == 0 and owner's balance increases via transfer); the mutant that transfers balance to address(0) instead will cause owner NOT to receive those funds for some inputs (nonzero msg.value), so observing owner's balance distinguishes them.

For any caller and any nonzero value sent to go(), after go() returns the contract balance is always zero and the owner address has a strictly greater ETH balance than before the call (reference preserves owner funds, mutant burns them); the mutant can violate the owner balance increase for some fuzzed value.

For every caller and amount, after calling go with a target that accepts and returns funds, the contract's balance is zero (all forwarded funds end up transferred out); the mutant that transfers the remaining balance to address(0) still leaves c.balance == 0 but breaks the invariant that the original owner address's balance increases when msg.value > 0 — therefore asserting that owner balance increased after go distinguishes them.

For every nonzero ETH amount and for any callee that accepts and returns funds (i.e. does not revert and simply forwards back the value), calling c.go() results in address(c).balance == 0 afterwards (the contract forwards/returns funds and then empties itself); the mutant that transfers the remaining balance to address(0) can cause address(c).balance != 0 during the call result flow only if the external callee behaves differently — but more robust distinguishing rule: for any nonzero ETH amount sent to go() when the external callee accepts funds, the owner's balance after the call strictly increases by the sent amount in the reference but not necessarily in the mutant — however EOAs as callees always succeed, so we deploy a helper that ACCEPTS and then RETURNS the funds to C to ensure the reference forwards back to owner; the mutant that burns the balance breaks that owner-balance-increase property for some fuzzed amount.

For any caller and any ETH amount, when c.go forwards ETH to a callee that returns the funds, the reference contract always results in the owner having at least the same balance as before plus the returned amount (owner balance increases), whereas the mutant that transfers to address(0) can leave the owner without that increase for some fuzzed amounts.

For any caller and any sent value, after go() returns the contract balance is zero (the reference forwards any remaining balance to owner); the mutant that transfers remaining balance to msg.sender can leave non-zero balance for some inputs (when the external call drains differently), so the property can be violated.

For every caller and any ETH value, after go() returns the contract's entire balance is forwarded to the deployer/owner; the mutant instead forwards the remaining balance to msg.sender for some inputs (when the external target call sends ETH back into the contract), so there exist inputs where owner does not receive the full balance and the property is broken.

For every caller and any sent ETH, after go() completes the contract balance is zero (all residual ETH is forwarded out); the mutant can leave a non-zero contract balance for some inputs when the external call to the provided target re-enters and sends ETH back into the contract, because it forwards remaining balance to msg.sender instead of owner.

For every caller and any payable amount sent to go(target), the reference contract always forwards any residual balance to the deployer-owned owner (so owner receives any leftover ETH), whereas the mutant forwards residual balance to msg.sender which for some adversarial target behavior causes owner to not receive that residual amount.

For any caller and any sent ETH amount, after go(...) completes the contract forwards any remaining balance to the deployer-owned owner (so address(c).balance == 0 and owner received funds); the mutant that forwards remaining balance to msg.sender can leave funds accessible to the caller for some adversarial target behavior, breaking this rule.

After any call to go() with any msg.value sent by any caller, the contract's entire remaining balance is forwarded to the stored owner (so address(c).balance == 0); the mutant instead may leave a non-zero balance in c by transferring leftovers to target rather than owner when the external call succeeds, breaking the zero-balance rule for some inputs.

For every admissible call to go by any caller with any nonzero msg.value where the external target call succeeds, the contract forwards any leftover balance to the owner so that owner’s received balance increases by the msg.value (i.e., owner ends up richer by the value sent); the mutant sending leftovers to target can cause the owner's balance to be less than expected for some inputs.

For any caller and any msg.value, after calling go() the contract's balance is always zero (the reference forwards any leftovers to owner); the mutant can leave a non-zero balance by transferring leftovers to the target instead and thus can violate address(c).balance == 0 for some inputs.

For any caller and any nonzero ether amount sent to C.go, the reference forwards the same amount to the external target causing C's balance to be zero after the call; the mutant that calls the target with value 0 can leave leftover ether in C (address(c).balance > 0) for some inputs.

For every caller and every nonzero msg.value, after calling go the contract's balance is zero (the sent value is forwarded out); the mutant that always forwards 0 can leave a nonzero balance for some inputs, so address(c).balance == 0 is violated.

For every caller and every nonzero msg.value, if the callee target's fallback accepts and does not keep funds (it forwards or otherwise results in C's balance returning to zero), then after go() completes C's balance is equal to zero; the mutant that calls the target with value 0 can leave C with a nonzero balance for some msg.value sent by the caller when the target's fallback accepts value, so address(c).balance == 0 is violated for those inputs.

For every caller and amount, after calling go through a callee that reverts, the reference C never transfers the sent ETH to owner (owner balance unchanged) because it forwards msg.value to the external call which reverts, whereas the mutant that transfers contract balance to owner before calling the external target can transfer the ETH to owner for some inputs; the test asserts owner balance is unchanged after go routed through a reverting helper.
